# Page 1^page=1
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.63 10 Sylow’s Theorems Humanity is on the cusp of knowing all the symmetries of every possible shape (in this universe, or any other universe!). A fundamental tool for this are Sylow’s Theorems. Peter Ludwig Sylow (1832–1918) was a Norwegian mathematician with a great sense of humour who liked the outdoors. Motivation. Lagrange’s Theorem allows us to say what orders of subgroups are impossible. For example, if ∣G∣ = 72 ⋅ 3 then G has no subgroup of order 3. We already that the converse to Lagrange’s Theorem doesn’t hold: A4 has no subgroup of order 6, even though ∣A4∣ = 12. Sylow’s Theorems are a partial converse to Lagrange’s Theorem. They tell us for example, that if ∣G∣ = 72 ⋅ 3 then G has a subgroup of order 7 2. 10.1 The Sylow Theorems Definition 10.1.1. If p is a prime, and H is a group of order pr, for some r, then we say that H is a p group. If H is a subgroup of another group G, then we say H is a p-subgroup of G. Example 10.1.2. (i) The group C9 is a 3 group because it’s order is a power of 3. It is a 3-subgroup of S9. (ii) The group S9 is not a p group for any prime p, since its order is not a prime power. (iii) The Klein 4-group K4 is a 2-group, because its order is a power of 2. It is a 2-subgroup of S4. Definition 10.1.3. Let G be a finite group. For any prime number p that divides ∣G∣, we can write ∣G∣ = p rt, with p ∤ t (i.e. p does not divide t) A Sylow p-subgroup of G is a subgroup H ≤ G such that ∣H∣ = pr. We will also call these p-Sylow subgroup. [Note: a p-Sylow subgroup of G is the largest p-subgroup of G.] Example 10.1.4. S5 has order ∣S5∣ = 5! = 23 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 5. Taking p = 2 we can write ∣S5∣ = 2 3 ⋅ 15, and we check that 2 ∤ 15. Any subgroup of S5 that has order 2 3 = 8 is then a Sylow 2-subgroup of S5. Note that subgroups of S5 of order 2 or 4 are 2-subgroups of S5, but not 2-Sylow subgroups of S5. Theorem 10.1.5. (First Sylow Theorem) Let G be a finite group. If prime p divides ∣G∣, then G has at least one Sylow p-subgroup H. Theorem 10.1.6. (Second Sylow Theorem) Let G be a finite group with p-Sylow subgroup H. If J is any p-subgroup of G [Note: J is not necessarily a p-Sylow subgroup] then J ≤ g−1Hg for some g ∈ G. Theorem 10.1.7. (Third Sylow Theorem) Let G be a finite group and let a(p) be the number of p-Sylow subgroups of G. Then: (i) a(p) divides t (where ∣G∣ = p r ⋅ t, with t and p coprime) and (ii) a(p) ≡ 1 mod p What is the point?!. Why are these so important? Well the first theorem tells us that every finite group has a p-Sylow subgroup for each prime p dividing ∣G∣, the second tells us how they are all related, and the third tells us how many there are. Using them, we can often determine all the groups of a given order. Amazing! Remark 10.1.8. Sylow’s First Theorem is a generalisation of Cauchy’s Theorem, which states that if G is a finite group and p is a prime number dividing ∣G∣, then G contains a subgroup of order p. Question 10.1.9. Let G be a group of order 54. Use Sylow’s Theorems to prove that G has a subgroup H of order 27 and a subgroup K of order 2. This is easy! Since ∣G∣ = 3 3 ⋅ 2, any 3-Sylow subgroup of G has order 3 3 = 27, and any 2-Sylow subgroup of G has order 2. By Sylow’s First Theorem, G has a 3-Sylow subgroup and a 2-Sylow subgroup.

# Page 2^page=2
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.64 10.1.1 Handout for Section 10.1 Example 10.1.10. What are some Sylow subgroups of D10? Well ∣D10∣ = 10 = 21 ⋅ 51. Hence D10 has 5-Sylow subgroups and 2-Sylow subgroups. The 5-Sylow subgroups have order 5 1 = 5. For example, ⟨(12345)⟩ is a 5-Sylow subgroup of D10. It is isomorphic to C5. You should check yourself, but C2 is a 2-Sylow subgroup of D10. In fact, up to isomorphism, these are the only Sylow subgroups of D10. Example 10.1.11. What are some Sylow subgroups of S6? Well ∣S6∣ = 6! = 24 ⋅ 32 ⋅ 5. Therefore, the 3-Sylow subgroups of S6 have order 3 2 = 9, the 2-Sylow subgroups have order 2 4 and the 5-Sylow subgroups have order 5. • C5 is a 5-Sylow subgroup of S6. • ⟨(123)⟩ × ⟨(456)⟩ ≅ C3 × C3 is a subgroup of S6. Also ∣C3 × C3∣ = 3 ⋅ 3 = 9. Hence, C3 × C3 is a 3-Sylow subgroup of S6. • ⟨(1 2)⟩ ≅ C2 is not a 2-Sylow subgroup of S6, because 2-Sylow subgroups of S6 must have order 2 4.

# Page 3^page=3
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.65 10.2 Applying Sylow’s Theorems Example 10.2.1. We will now prove that every group of order 162 has a normal subgroup H of order 81. Claim 1: There is a subgroup H of G with order 81. Proof: well ∣G∣ = 34 ⋅ 2, so any 3-Sylow subgroup of G has order 34. By Sylow’s First Theorem, there is a 3-Sylow subgroup H of G. Claim 2: H is the only 3-Sylow subgroup of G. The number a(3) of 3-Sylow subgroups in G satisfies a(3)∣2 and a(3) ≡ 1 mod 3 by Sylow’s Third Theorem. Now a(3)∣2 implies a(3) = 1 or 2, and a(3) ≡ 1 mod 3 implies a(3) ∈ {1, 4, 7, 10, . . .}. Hence a(3) = 1. Claim 3: H ⊴ G. Fix g ∈ G. We will show that g−1Hg = H. First, note that g−1Hg is a subgroup of G by the Quick Subgroup Test [Identity: obvious. Closure: (g−1h1g)(g−1h2g) = g−1h1h2g ∈ g−1Hg. Inverse: (g−1hg)(g−1h −1g) = e]. Also ∣g−1Hg∣ = ∣H∣. Therefore g−1Hg is a 3-Sylow subgroup of G. Since G has only one 3-Sylow subgroup (by Claim 2), we have g−1Hg = H. Example 10.2.2. We will now prove that every group of order 15 is cyclic using Sylow’s theorems. Let G be a group with ∣G∣ = 15. Notice that ∣G∣ = 15 = 3 1 ⋅ 51. Claim 1: A subgroup of G can only have orders 1, 3, 5 and 15. Proof: by Lagrange’s Theorem. Claim 2: G has only one subgroup of order 1. Proof: obvious—it’s ⟨eG⟩ by Proposi- tion 2.2.6. Claim 3: G has only one subgroup of order 15. Proof: obvious—it’s G by Proposition 2.2.6. Claim 4: G has only one subgroup of order 3. Proof: By the First Sylow Theorem, we know that G has at least one 3-Sylow subgroup H, with ∣H∣ = 3 1 = 3. Notice that every 3-subgroup of G is a 3-Sylow subgroup, because ∣G∣ = 3 1 ⋅ 51. By the Third Sylow Theorem, a(3) ∣ 5 and a(p) ≡ 1 mod 3. First fact means a(3) = 1, 5 and second fact means a(3) = 1. So, there is only one 3-subgroup of G. Claim 5: G has only one subgroup of order 5. Proof: As above, every 5-subgroup of G is a 5-Sylow subgroup, and a(5) = 1 or 3, with a(5) ≡ 1 mod 5, so a(5) = 1. Claim 6: G is cyclic. Proof: Let J be the unique 3-subgroup of G, and let K be the unique 5-subgroup. The only subgroups of G are thus ⟨eG⟩, J, K, G. Note that (because eG ∈ J ∩ K) there are at most 1 + (3 − 1) + (5 − 1) = 7 elements of G that lie in ⟨eG⟩ or J or K. Choose some g ∈ G that is not in any of them. Now ⟨g⟩ ≤ G, but it can’t equal ⟨eG⟩, J or K because none of these contain g. Hence ⟨g⟩ = G.

# Page 4^page=4
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.66 10.3 Handout: Proof of the First Sylow Theorem (not exam- inable) It is important that you fully understand this proof, however you will not be required to repeat the entirety of this proof in an examination. Let us first recall the theorem. First Sylow Theorem. Let G be a finite group. If prime p divides ∣G∣, then G has at least one Sylow p-subgroup H. Proof of Sylow’s First Theorem. Write ∣G∣ = p rt, where p and t are coprime and r ≥ 1. Idea: We will look at subsets of G that have size p r, and we will see that the stabiliser of one of them is a subgroup of G and has size p r. This will be the p-Sylow subgroup of G we are looking for. Let X ∶= {W ⊆ G ∶ ∣W ∣ = pr} be the set of all of these subsets. Now ∣X∣ equals the number of ways of choosing pr from p rt, therefore: ∣X∣ = ( prt pr ) = prt pr ⋅ (p rt − 1) (p r − 1) ⋯ (p rt − i) (p r − i) ⋯ (p rt − (p r − 1)) 1 . Claim: p ∤ ∣X∣. Proof: if p h divides some term (p rt − i), then p h ∣ i. Hence ph divides (pr − i). But this means that any p h factor in a numerator is matched by a ph factor in the denominator, so they cancel. Thus p does not divide ∣X∣. Now X is a G-set, with λ(g)W = gW for all g ∈ G and all W ∈ X. Let W1, . . . , Wa be representatives of the orbits of G on X, so X = GW1 ∪ . . . ∪ GWa. Therefore, ∣X∣ = ∣GW1∣ + ⋯∣GWa∣. Since p ∤ ∣X∣, there is some orbit GWi such that p ∤ ∣GWi∣. Let S ∶= StabG(Wi). We will prove that S is a p-Sylow subgroup of G. Now S ≤ G by Proposition 9.1.0, so all we need to prove is that ∣S∣ = p r. By the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem (Theorem 9.1.1), ∣GWi∣ = ∣G∣/∣S∣. Since S ≤ G, we know that ∣S∣ divides ∣G∣ by Lagrange’s Theorem. Since ∣G∣ = p rt, we have ∣S∣ = pks for some k ≤ r and s ∣ t. However, p does not divide ∣GWi∣, so we must have ∣S∣ = prs. Claim: ∣S∣ ≤ ∣Wi∣. Proof: fix any w ∈ Wi and consider the orbit Sw = {gw ∶ g ∈ S}. If ∣S∣ > ∣Sw∣ then gw = hw for distinct g, h ∈ S. However, since w ∈ G we have gww−1 = hww−1, so g = h. This is a contradiction. Hence ∣S∣ ≤ ∣Sw∣. Furthermore, Sw ⊆ Wi because S is the stabiliser of Wi, so ∣Sw∣ ≤ ∣Wi∣. Therefore ∣S∣ ≤ ∣Wi∣ as claimed. Using our claim, we have p rs = ∣S∣ ≤ ∣Wi∣ = pr, so s = 1. Hence ∣S∣ = pr. Thus S is a p-Sylow subgroup of G.

# Page 5^page=5
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.67 [Advanced handout: You are NOT required to read this, it is here just in case you are interested] Proof of the Second and Third Sylow Theorems (not examinable) First, a definition that we will need. Definition 10.3.1. Let G be a group and h ∈ G. The centraliser of h in G is defined to be CG(h) = {g ∈ G ∶ g−1hg = h}. For a subset S ⊆ G a similar object NG(S) is called the normaliser of S in G, and is defined to be NG(S) = {g ∈ G ∶ g−1Sg = S} (These objects will play a role in some 4th year courses.) Notice that when a group acts on itself by conjugation, we have that λ(g)x = gxg−1; hence the stabiliser of x under this action is {g ∈ G ∶ gxg−1 = x} = {g ∈ G ∶ x = g−1xg} = CG(x). The orbits of this action are called the conjugacy classes of G. Second Sylow Theorem. Let G be a finite group with p-Sylow subgroup H. If J is any p-subgroup of G [Note: J is not necessarily a p-Sylow subgroup] then J ≤ g−1Hg for some g ∈ G. Proof of Sylow’s Second Theorem. Recall that G/H is the set of cosets of H in G, and G acts on Y = G/H by left multiplication, so λ(g)(g′H) = gg′H for all g ∈ G and all g′H ∈ Y . Since J ≤ G, this means λ is also an action of J on Y . Since J acts on Y , this means Y can be partitioned into orbits. Let FixY(J) be the set of points in Y that are fixed by every element in J. Points in Y lie in orbits of size one. Hence we can write Y = FixY(J) ∪ Orb1 ∪ . . . ∪ Orbm, where all the sets in the union are pairwise disjoint and all orbits have size at least 2. Now ∣J∣ is a power of p, and the Orbit Stabiliser Theorem tells us that the size of each orbit divides ∣J∣. Therefore, ∣Y ∣ = ∣FixY(J)∣ + pk1 + . . . + p km , for some k1, . . . , km ∈ N. Now ∣Y ∣ = [G ∶ H], and [G ∶ H] is coprime to p because H is a p-Sylow subgroup of G. Hence we must have that ∣FixY(J)∣ ≥ 1. Since ∣FixY(J)∣ ≥ 1, we can choose some gH ∈ Y such that λ(a)gH = gH for all a ∈ J. Hence agH = gH, and therefore a ∈ gHg−1. Since this is true for all a ∈ J we have that J ⊆ g−1Hg. Since J and g−1Hg are groups, it then follows that J ≤ g−1Hg. Third Sylow Theorem. Let G be a finite group and let a(p) be the number of p-Sylow subgroups of G. Then: (i) a(p) divides t (where ∣G∣ = p r ⋅ t, with t and p coprime) and (ii) a(p) ≡ 1 mod p Proof of Sylow’s Third Theorem. Let Y be the set of all p-Sylow subgroups of G. Then ∣Y ∣ = a(p). For all g ∈ G and H ∈ Y we have that gHg−1 is also a p-Sylow subgroup of G, and hence gHg−1 ∈ Y . It is easy to see that we have an action λ of G on Y given by λ(g)H = gHg−1, for all g ∈ G and all H ∈ Y . By Sylow’s Second Theorem, we know that G has only one orbit on Y . Therefore Y = Gy for all y ∈ Y . By the Orbit Stabiliser Theorem, a(p) = ∣Y ∣ = ∣Gy∣ = ∣G∣/∣StabG(y)∣, and so in particular, a(p) divides ∣G∣. (3)

# Page 6^page=6
Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.68 We now show that a(p) ≡ 1 mod p. Fix J ∈ Y . Since J ≤ G this means that λ is also an action of J on Y . As we did in the proof of Sylow’s Second Theorem, we can write Y as a union of orbits and use the Orbit Stabiliser Theorem to show that ∣Y ∣ = ∣FixY(J)∣ + pk1 + . . . + p km , for some k1, . . . , km ∈ N. Hence, since ∣Y ∣ = a(p), a(p) ≡ ∣FixY(J)∣ mod p. Claim: FixY(J) = {J}. Proof: first note that it is obvious that J ∈ FixY(J). Suppose H ∈ Y is some element in FixY(J). Then for all a ∈ J we have aHa −1 = H. Of course we can also write this as H = a−1Ha. Recall (from Definition 10.3.1) that the normaliser of H in G is NG(H) = {g ∈ G ∶ g−1Hg = H}. It is easy to see (using the Quick Subgroup Test) that NG(H) ≤ G. Now H ≤ NG(H) and J ≤ NG(H), so H and J are two p-Sylow subgroups of NG(H). We can apply Sylow’s Second Theorem to NG(H) to deduce that H and J satisfy, J ≤ g−1Hg, for some g ∈ NG(H). However, by the definition of NG(H), we know that g−1Hg = H. Therefore J ≤ H. Since ∣J∣ = ∣H∣ we therefore have that J = H. Hence FixY(J) = {J} and our claim is true. By our claim, we see that ∣FixY(J)∣ = 1, and therefore, a(p) ≡ 1 mod p. (4) By (3) above we have that a(p) divides ∣G∣ = prt, and so a(p) = p ks for some k ≤ r and some s that divides t. On the other hand, by (4) above we have that a(p) is coprime to p. Hence a(p) = s and so a(p) divides t.
